I will keep my land in the usual Quzhou two-crop system: winter wheat first, then summer maize on the same ground. I am in southern Hebei, and Quzhou’s climate is dry and windy in spring but gets most of its rain in July to September, so wheat-maize rotation still matches the weather and the way I farm here. At my age, I want a system I already know, that can be handled with machines, does not depend on too much hired labor, and still gives me stable grain output. I will not switch into labor-heavy cash crops this year.

I will manage the wheat more carefully in spring because that is where drought risk is biggest. I will keep fertilizer moderate instead of pushing it too hard, follow a few key irrigations, and spray only when disease, weeds, or insects justify it. After wheat harvest, I will go straight into summer maize with a hybrid seed, mostly no-tillage/direct seeding, because that saves time, protects moisture, and fits the local pattern well. I am setting my targets below the best demonstration fields but still aiming for solid yields with lower risk. I’m basing that on Quzhou local climate and county wheat-maize work from China Agricultural University’s Quzhou station and county demonstration results: [曲周实验站地理位置](https://qzsyz.cau.edu.cn/col/col46277/index.html), [2024主推技术](https://qzsyz.cau.edu.cn/art/2024/2/25/art_46232_1012984.html), [曲周“吨半粮”示范结果](https://qzsyz.cau.edu.cn/art/2024/10/8/art_46317_1039835.html).
